meta.title: Running VLAs at Real-time Speed
meta.subtitle: 让十亿参数的视觉-语言-动作模型在消费级 GPU 上实时运行
meta.authors: Yunchao Ma, Yizhuang Zhou, Yunhuan Yang, Tiancai Wang, Haoqiang Fan
meta.field: 具身智能 · 机器人控制

why_read.title: 为什么值得读
why_read.intro: 在动手拆解之前，先搞清楚：这件事为什么重要，为什么有人愿意花大力气去做。

blocks.text: 学习式机器人控制正在普及，尤其是十亿参数级的 VLA 模型（Vision-Language-Action，视觉-语言-动作模型：一种能「看」图像、「听」语言指令、直接「输出」机器人动作的 AI）。它泛化能力惊人，却普遍面临「延迟」问题——做一次前向推理（把输入算成输出的完整计算过程，相当于模型「思考一次」）就要几百毫秒。
很多真实任务要求极快的反应：比如接住一个正在下落的物体。模型「思考」一次要几百毫秒，物体早就掉到地上了。
关键门槛是 33 毫秒（约 1/30 秒）：只有快过它，才能完整处理 30 FPS 视频流（每秒 30 帧）的每一帧。哪怕慢到 34 毫秒，也得偶尔「丢帧」——关键事件一旦落在被丢的那一帧上，反应就多延迟整整一帧。
一句话：这篇论文想打破「大模型聪明但慢，所以做不了实时任务」这个成见。它值得读的地方不在新算法，而在它怎么把「快不起来」这个模糊焦虑，拆成一个个可测量、可逐个解决的工程问题。

prior_work.title: 以前怎么解决
prior_work.intro: 「让机器人又快又聪明」不是新问题。看看前人走过的路。

blocks.text: 传统机器人控制分三层，不同算法跑在不同频率：底层力/力矩控制（直接控制关节力度）跑在 1kHz（每秒 1000 次）级别的高频，反应快但不理解语义；而 VLA 被认为只能做「慢而聪明」的中层控制（负责理解任务、规划动作）。

在「让模型跑得更快」这条技术线上，前人积累了大量工具：手工优化的 kernel（GPU 上执行的一小段计算任务，相当于流水线上的一个工序，如 XLA、TensorRT、CUTLASS）、调度型编译器（自动安排计算顺序的工具，如 TVM）、超优化搜索（自动寻找最优实现，如 Mirage、Neptune），以及 FlashAttention、FlashDecoding 这类「省内存搬运」的注意力优化。
这些方法的共同思路是：减少 kernel 数量、减少显存（GPU 的内存）搬运、把多个计算合并成一个。它们都有效，但各有侧重、没人把它们系统性地用全。

prior_limits.title: 为什么以前不够
prior_limits.intro: 工具这么多，为什么 VLA 还是「快不起来」？

blocks.text: FlashAttention / FlashDecoding 只优化了注意力这一块，却忽略了 FFN（Transformer 里除注意力之外的另一大块计算）等其他部分；整个前向过程仍要启动很多次 kernel、反复访问 DRAM（显存里较慢的那层内存），开销还是大。
TensorRT 等自动编译框架虽然省事，但面对 VLA 这种「一次推理要跑一千多个 kernel」的大模型，仍留下大量 CPU 派发开销（CPU 逐个下令启动 kernel 的时间）和重复的显存访问，达不到实时要求。
最朴素的 PyTorch 实现更是慢到 105 毫秒（单视角）——CPU 要逐条驱动上千个 kernel，光「下令」这一步就拖垮了延迟。
换句话说：以前不是没有工具，而是没人把这些工具**系统性、按顺序**地用到 VLA 上，也没有人先去量一量「理论上到底还能快多少」。

position.title: 这篇论文处在哪
position.intro: 把它放进坐标系里：它既不发明新模型，也不发明新优化工具，那它的位置在哪？

blocks.text: 在「又快又聪明」这条轴线上，本文是突破点：它第一次证明 π0 级别（π0 是一个知名的开源 VLA 模型）的十亿参数 VLA，能在单张消费级 GPU（普通玩家买得起的显卡，而非数据中心专用卡）上实时运行——30Hz 帧率，最高 480Hz 力控频率。

在「加速方法」这条轴线上，它不造新轮子，而是把 CUDA graph（一种把 GPU 上成百上千个小任务打包、一次性重放、从而省掉 CPU 逐个下令开销的机制）、计算图变换、Triton kernel 调优（Triton 是一种方便手写高效 GPU 代码的语言）、roofline 下界分析（roofline 是估算计算性能理论上限的工具，像给 GPU 算力画一条天花板线）这些已有手段，整合成一条针对 VLA 的完整管线。
所以它的独特贡献是「整合 + 系统化」：把「能不能实时」从经验猜测，变成「用理论下界论证，证明已接近最优」的工程结论。

guess.title: 如果是你，你会怎么办
guess.intro: 现在把论文挡起来。你已知这些约束——如果是你，怎么把推理从 100+ms 压到 33ms 以内？
constraints: 模型是 π0 级别：约 3B 参数的 VLM（视觉语言模型，负责「看」和「理解」）+ 300M 参数的动作专家（负责「输出动作」），结构固定，不能换成小模型。
只能在一张消费级 RTX 4090 显卡上跑，不能靠云端多卡并行。
目标：从 100 多毫秒压到 33 毫秒以内（匹配 30 FPS）。

scaffold.text: 换一个更小、更快的模型来跑
scaffold.why: 这违背论文核心主张——「大模型也能实时」。缩水模型是回避问题，不是解决问题。

scaffold.text: 系统性优化推理管线：消除 CPU 开销 + 简化计算图 + 手工调优 kernel
scaffold.why: 这正是作者路线：CUDA graph 消 CPU 开销、图变换删冗余计算、Triton 调优矩阵乘，三层递进。

scaffold.text: 把推理搬到云端，用多张卡并行加速
scaffold.why: 论文明确要求「单张消费级 GPU」，云端多卡违背了「单卡实时」的设定。

scaffold.text: 大幅降低图像分辨率、减少输入帧数来省时间
scaffold.why: 这是「偷工减料」。作者方向相反——还想支持更多视角、更高帧率。

solution.title: 作者怎么解决
solution.intro: 答案揭晓：作者没发明新模型，而是把「推理」当成一个可逐层优化的工程问题，一层层把开销抠掉。

chain.text: 33ms 内反应，单张 4090，模型不能改。
从最朴素 PyTorch 的 105ms 逐项计时，再用 roofline 模型（估算性能理论上限的工具）算出理论下界（2 视角约 19.7ms）。
CPU 开销、计算图冗余、单个 kernel 低效——三类，清晰可数。
CUDA graph → 图简化 → Triton 调优，层层递进，每步都有计时数据支撑。

blocks.text: 第一层消除 CPU 开销：用 CUDA graph 把 1000 多个 kernel 的「启动流程」录制下来交给 GPU 一次性重放（想象把散装零件打包成标准件，省掉 CPU 逐个下令的时间），绕开 Python 逐条派发，约提速 2 倍。
第二层简化计算图：折叠 RMS norm（一种让数值稳定的归一化层）的仿射参数、折叠 action-time embedding（给动作打时间标签的模块）的线性层、把 QKV 投影（注意力机制里把输入变成「查询/键/值」三组向量的变换）合并成一个大矩阵乘，结果等价但省约 7-8ms。
第三层深入 kernel：用 Triton 手工调优 GEMM（矩阵乘法，深度学习最核心的运算）的分块参数、融合 gated linear 层、把 bias/残差/激活这些零碎计算融进矩阵乘，再省约 8ms。
最终结果：2 视角推理从 openpi/jax（一种官方实现）的 53.7ms 降到 27.3ms，跨过 30 FPS 门槛；最朴素 PyTorch 的 105ms 被压到 20ms（1 视角）。
注意作者的节奏：先摘「低垂果实」（收益大、改动小），再啃「硬骨头」（单 kernel 深度优化），并用 roofline 下界告诉自己「还剩最多 30% 空间」——这是典型的工程方法论，不是天才灵光。

experiment.title: 实验到底证明了什么
experiment.intro: 论文没停在跑分，而是做了真实世界验证。关键要想清楚：这个实验**到底证明了什么，又没证明什么**。

blocks.text: 实验设计：两个上下对齐的夹爪夹住一支笔，上方夹爪松开后，下方夹爪要在正确时机闭合接住它。夹爪开合仅 60ms（约两帧画面），而且相机看不到上方夹爪，无法直接观察松手时刻——系统必须靠「预判」而非「看到」来抓。
相机是 30 FPS 的 720P USB 相机，测量延迟约两帧（一帧在 ISP——相机把原始信号转成图像的环节，一帧在 USB 传输）；笔要下落约 30cm 才被接住。训练数据：600 个 episode（一段完整的示范轨迹），用官方 openpi 仓库训练。
结果：连续 10 次实验全部成功（100%），端到端反应 <200ms。作者还做了人类对照：人接住他人手中落下的笔，30cm 已是反应距离下限，说明系统的反应速度与人类相当。
但要看清边界：作者自己承认「从学习角度看这结果很 trivial（微不足道），LeNet 甚至 SVM 这类简单模型也能做到」——所以这个实验证明的是**系统延迟**达标，而不是**模型能力**有多强。

limitation.title: 还有什么问题
limitation.intro: 先别急着看作者的自我批评，你自己先挑毛病：这套方法有什么软肋？

scaffold.text: 优化高度依赖特定硬件（RTX 4090）和特定模型（π0），迁移到别的硬件/模型要重新调优
scaffold.why: tile 参数、partial split-k（矩阵乘的拆分策略）、roofline 参数都针对 4090 这块卡标定，换硬件要重做。

scaffold.text: 480Hz 力控闭环只是框架设想，没有实际实现和验证
scaffold.why: Full Streaming Inference（完整流式推理框架）全文只是设计草图，作者明确说实现细节省略、留待后续。

scaffold.text: 抓笔任务太简单，不能证明复杂任务上的实时能力
scaffold.why: 作者亲口承认从学习角度微不足道，实验只验证延迟、不验证能力。

scaffold.text: 优化后模型精度明显下降
scaffold.why: 论文没报告精度下降——这是「无法确定」，不能当成已成立的缺陷。

author_limitations.text: 「From a learning perspective, this result is trivial」——作者承认任务太简单，真正贡献在系统/延迟而非算法/精度。
Full Streaming Inference（480Hz 力控 + 30Hz 视觉 + <1Hz 文本三环）只是设计草图，实现细节全部省略。
software barrier（软件同步屏障，一种省同步开销的做法）融合实测反而变慢，只用作「同步开销下界」的论证工具，未真正采用。
partial split-k 收益不到 0.1ms，作者自评是「有趣的案例」而非关键贡献。

future.title: 后续论文怎么继续
future.intro: 一篇好论文会自己指出「下一步往哪走」。看作者怎么给自己铺路。

blocks.text: 硬件换代：RTX 5090 提供 1.79TB/s 带宽（每秒能搬运的数据量）和更多算力，作者预计 7B 参数模型会是下一个里程碑，60-120 FPS 的视觉延迟成为可能方向。
框架落地：把 480Hz 的 Full Streaming Inference 真正实现并验证，触及实时力控（直接高频控制力度）的门槛。
能力升级：引入 VLM（视觉语言模型）作为 System I（借鉴认知科学里「快思考」的概念，负责直觉式的高层反应）做高层场景感知与任务规划，引入力觉、视觉触觉等多感官信息，处理更复杂的实时任务。
数据挑战：若追求 >480Hz 的更高控制频率，每秒要收集上千级演示数据，这本身也是难题。

next_question.title: 下一个研究问题是什么
next_question.intro: 训练的最高目标不是记住结论，而是你能从这里长出自己的问题。论文已经给了线索，试着把它变成「你的」下一个研究问题。
prompts: 论文承认抓笔任务「微不足道」，那什么样的实时任务才能真正暴露 VLA 的能力上限？
方法强依赖 RTX 4090，能不能让这套优化「可移植」到不同硬件而不重新手调？
480Hz 力控还是草图——你能否设计一个实验，证明「更高频率的力控」真的带来任务收益？
如果把「又快」和「聪明」结合：高频力控 + 高层 VLM 规划，中间该怎么分工？

blocks.text: 一个通用的思考框架：从「局限」出发，把每个「不能/没做」翻译成一个可验证的问题，就是论文最诚实的下一步。

timeline_domain.title: 传统控制：高频但「不聪明」
timeline_domain.text: 力控/扭矩控制在 1kHz 级别做精确控制，反应极快，但缺乏语义理解与泛化。

timeline_domain.title: VLA 兴起：聪明但「慢」
timeline_domain.text: π0 等十亿参数 VLA（视觉-语言-动作模型）带来强泛化，但单次推理数百毫秒，被认为只能做「慢而聪明」的中层控制。

timeline_domain.title: 本文：又快又聪明
timeline_domain.text: 证明 VLA 也能跑 30Hz、最高 480Hz 力控频率，打破「大模型无法实时」的成见。

timeline_tech.title: 朴素 PyTorch
timeline_tech.text: Python 逐条派发 CUDA kernel（GPU 上的一小段计算任务），kernel 一多，CPU 派发开销就成了大头。

timeline_tech.title: 编译优化：XLA / TensorRT / TVM
timeline_tech.text: 通过算子调度、融合、自动调优减少 kernel 数量与显存搬运。

timeline_tech.title: Triton
timeline_tech.text: 一种方便手写高效 GPU 代码的语言，把张量拆成 tile（小块）直接映射到硬件，让非专家也能写高效 kernel。

timeline_tech.title: FlashAttention
timeline_tech.text: IO-aware 注意力实现，用分块减少 HBM（高带宽显存）↔SRAM（更快的片上内存）之间的搬运。

timeline_tech.title: CUDA graph
timeline_tech.text: 录制并重放 kernel 流，彻底消除 CPU launch 开销——本文的第一层武器。

timeline_tech.title: 本文：系统化应用到 VLA
timeline_tech.text: 把上述手段整合成完整管线，并用 roofline 下界论证「接近最优」。

Abstract
In this paper, we show how to run π0-levelmulti-view
VLA at30Hzframe rate and at most480Hztrajectory fre-
quency using a single consumer GPU. This enables dy-
namic and real-time tasks that were previously believed to
be unattainable by large VLA models. To achieve it, we
introduce a bag of strategies to eliminate the overheads
in model inference. The real-world experiment shows that
the π0 policy with our strategy achieves a100%success
rate in grasping a falling pen task. Based on the results,
we further propose a full streaming inference framework
for real-time robot control of VLA. Code is available at
https://github.com/Dexmal/realtime-vla.
1. Introduction
Learning-based robotic control algorithms are prevailing,
especially billion-parameter VLA models [2, 3, 16, 18]. De-
spite their impressive generalization, these models face a
latency issue. Many real-world tasks, such as grasping a mov-
ing object, tend to require a quick reaction time. However, a
forward pass of VLA models typically requires hundreds of
milliseconds, impeding quick reactions that were expected
from a dynamic robot. Running less than 33 ms ≈1/30 s

every now and then during continuous operation. If the event
we need to detect happens to occur at the dropped frame, the

In this paper, we make a crucial observation that VLAs
are indeed capable of running in real-time under a single con-
sumer RTX 4090 GPU. After our optimization, we achieve a
latency of 27.3 ms given two input views, significantly faster
than “official” inference provided by theopenpi [2] project
(See Tab. 1). The performance gain comes from our engi-
neering of the inference pipeline. First, we use the CUDA
graph approach to eliminate all CPU overheads. Then we
make transformations on the computational graph to reduce
the total MAC workload or the number of kernel launches.

===== 第 2 页 =====
After that, we rearrange the memory and tensor operations
inside individual kernels to better exploit parallelism. With
all of the above strategies, we successfully push inference
time to 30 FPS and above, meeting the demand for real-time
control.
To verify the effectiveness of our real-time strategy, we
design a simple proof-of-concept experiment in real world.
As shown in Fig. 1, two vertically aligned grabbers are made
to hold a marker pen. After the first grabber above releases
the pen, the second grabber is required to catch the pen at
the right time. Hundreds of grasping data is collected by au-
tomatic rules. Theπ0 model is trained to control the grabber
to grasp a pen falling from a higher disturbed position. Such
a task has a very stringent time constraint. During model
inference, theπ0 model achieves a 100% success rate on the
job thanks to the largely optimized inference time.
This result encourages us to rethink how to adopt the
VLAs into a real-time robot system. Currently, the robotic
control system mainly includes three layers and there are
different algorithms operating with a hierarchy of control
frequencies. The VLAs are believed to live in the layer of
mid-level control. Controls of higher frequencies, namely
force or torque control, are believed to be handled by other
algorithms. However, we find that the VLA itself contains
different tiers of input and output frequencies. We directly
map the structure of VLA into a full control algorithm and
call it the Full Streaming Inference mode. The system is
capable of generating control signals at maximum 480 Hz.
It touches the threshold of real-time force control.
Extending our framework to do more challenging real-
time tasks remains for future researchers. Researches may
further introduce the vision-language model (VLM) as the
System I on top of VLA part with 1-10 Hz frequency for
high-level scene perception and task planning. They may
also consider introducing multi-sensory information, such as
force and visual-tactile, into the action expert for real-time
action chunking decoding.
2. Preliminary onπ 0-level Model
π0 [2] is an excellent vision-language-action (VLA) policy
for general robotic manipulation. Hybrid training on both
robotic and multimodal data is performed for open-world
generalization [3]. From the perspective of model architec-
ture, it mainly includes two parts: vision-language model
(VLM) and action expert (AE).
VLMbackbone is initialized with PaliGemma [ 1], which is
a multimodal model with 3B parameters. It is composed of
a vision encoder SigLIP [22] with 400M parameters and a
large language model (LLM) Gemma [19] with 2.6B param-
eters. The representations of PaliGemma are learned from
large-scale web-data pretraining, providing strong prior for
parallel action decoding of AE part below.

3. Eliminating the Overheads
In the following sections, we show a step-by-step procedure
to construct the inference program. Our starting point is
a plain pytorch nn.Module implementation that literally
follows the model structure. The measured running time is
above 100 ms, which is far from our goal. The first steps
we take focus on some “low hanging fruits” that drastically
speed up computation by getting rid of CPU overhead (the
“+cuda graph” entry in Fig. 2) and removing redundant com-
putation (the “+simplified graph” entry).
3.1. Removing CPU Overhead
Nowadays, neural network inference is commonly driven
by Python code that launches underlying CUDA kernels.
However, the Python part has significant overhead when the
number of kernels is large. Inπ0 model, the total number of
kernels launched per inference step is estimated to be more
than a thousand, which makes the CPU issue urgent.
There are several Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) or Just-In-Time
(JIT) compilation techniques available. However, we find the
simplest and most effective way is to use the CUDA graph
mechanism. In a CUDA graph, we can record the stream of

3.2. Simplifying the Graph
In the next step, we take a closer look at the network struc-
ture and spot some computation that can be rewritten in an
equivalent way but runs faster. In compiler literature this is
reminiscent to the “constant folding” technique, but in the
context of model inference there are more that we can do.
We list all transformations taken and explain them one by
one (see Fig. 3).
The first is to fuse the affine parameters in the RMS norm
layer [23] into the subsequent linear layer. Because both
operations are linear, we can use the associativity law to
modify the weights in the linear layer to achieve it. The
second is to fold the “action time encoder” in the action
expert. The action value is up-projected to 1024 dimensions
and concatenated with a projected timestep encoding vector.
The result is fed into another linear layer. For the action value
branch, we can fold the two consecutive kernels into one as
there is no nonlinearity between them. For the time branch,
as there are only 10 different time steps during inference, we
can tabulate the result of the linear layer and fuse it all the
way to the bias vector right before SiLU operation [9]. This
reduces the number of operators and also saves MACs. The
third is to fuse QKV projections together. We can combine
the matrices used in Q, K, and V , to a single large matrix
and get the individual results back by slicing the resulting
tensor. This reduces the number of kernels and increases
parallelization. We can also fuse RoPE [17] operation into
the matrix multiplication, and precompute the weights used
in RoPE. As shown in Fig. 2, these modifications reduce the
inference time by 7-8 ms.
3.3. Avoiding Other Overheads
There are other overheads outside the GPU part but are also
worth mentioning. The first is image resizing, which can be
as slow as several milliseconds if not implemented correctly.
For this part, we observe that most camera ISP support many
different output resolutions. Using a resolution that is close
to the desired 224×224, e.g. 240×320, helps with this issue.
Also, carefully writing the resize code by hand reduces in-
ference time significantly, since we find the implementation
of JAX version sub-optimal. We measure the time that per-
forming image resizing under correct implementation takes
less than 60us on desktop x86 CPU. In the rest of the paper,
we do not count the time.
In addition to image resizing, there are other tips for the
whole inference system. Copying data back and forth be-
tween CPU and GPU requires pinned memory for optimal
performance. Making all CPU buffers static can reduce jit-
ter. Using zero-copying to handle camera frames reduces
latency. This paper do not go further into these details as
they are out-of-scope of the paper, but we stress that careful
implementation in all parts of the system is crucial for an
end-to-end real-time system.

4.1. Tuning Tile Parameters of GEMM
The default pytorch implementation of matmul goes to
cuBLAS, which dispatches to compiled cutlass kernels ac-
cording to the matrix dimensions. However, some of the
kernels do not receive the optimal configuration. We manu-
ally tuned the tiling strategies using a Triton implementation
and tabulated the results in Tab. 2, saving about 1.5 ms from
Triton optimization. Note that transformer in LLM only runs
17 times, instead of 18, of attention and FFN layers in the
Table. It is because only the KV caches are passed to the AE,
so the features of the last layer is not required, which further
saves about 0.7 ms.
4.2. Fusing Gated Linear Layers
In the transformer part of the model, the FFN uses a gated
up-projection implementation. The feature is multiplied
by two different weights and the results are combined as
FC 1(x,w 1)·GELU(FC 2(x,w 2)). Here, w1 and w2 are
the weights for two fully-connected layers FCs . During
computation, these two matmuls can run parallel, and more
importantly, their load and store operations can be coalesced.
After loading one input tile, two weight tiles can be loaded
for computation. When the results are written back to mem-
ory, only the combined result is required to be written, which
reduces the memory operation time and improves tensor
utilization. In this step, inference performance is further
improved by 1.7 ms.
4.3. Partial Split-k
In the computation graph (see Fig. 4), a special GEMM
of size 512×1152×1152 is worth mentioning. The core
problem of this size is that when using 64×64 tile, there
will be 144 blocks. It is not a multiple of 128, which means
the blocks fail to be distributed to the 128 SMs in RTX 4090.
Using smaller blocks helps make the distribution more even,
but reduces overall efficiency. Further splitting along the K
dimension produces higher overhead.
Our observation is that we can split the GEMM into two
parts. The first is a 512×1152×1024 matmul, which can
be evenly distributed to the SMs using 64×64 tile. The
second is 512×1152×128 , which can be partitioned to the
128 SMs using 32×32 block and split-2 partition in the K
dimension. The two parts can be written in a single kernel
as they do not depend on each other. The performance gain
from this optimization is less than 0.1 ms, but we think it is
an interesting case for further study.

4.4. Fusing the Scalar Operations
After optimizing the GEMMs, it is time to deal with the
scalar operations. The bias, residual shortcut and activation
operations can be trivially combined into the GEMM. For
the RMS norm, we first compute the token-level stats into a
separate buffer. Then in the next GEMM, we divide the mul-
tiplied result by the corresponding factor after all accumu-
lations. These operation reduces the total memory footprint.
The gain in this step is hard to estimate, but we attribute the
remaining gain in Fig. 2, which measures roughly 4 ms.
5. Establishing Lower Bound
In this section, we show how far we are from an “ideal”
implementation. Our arguments are based on two parts: the
unavoidable time for the matrices, and the non-negligible
time of synchronization.
5.1. Roofline of the GEMMs
The basic approach is the “roofline” model, which lower
bounds the time of a computation by the maximum of doing
all memory operations and all compute operations. In the
context of model inference, this translates to calculation of
the HBM bandwidth and tensor core cycles.
For one BF16 GEMM operation of dimensionN×K×M ,
the lower-bound is as follows:

matrix and the resultant matrix are usually the activation fea-

parameters on the other hand, are too large to be fully cached
so we should account for it.

We need to note that it is tricky to sum two consecutive

not affect the roofline argument for most cases. Thus, it is
proper to use the sum-of-parts approach.
5.2. Synchronization Overhead
We notice that there are a large number of kernels launched
in the CUDA stream. For data consistency, the SMs need to
wait for others to complete one kernel before launching the
next, which produces synchronization overhead.
There are totally 1378 matmuls show in Fig. 4 and an
experiment is performed to estimate the synchronization
overhead. We run a simple kernel for 1378 times and we
write one kernel that runs the computation inside a for loop
for the same amount of time without any synchronization, as
comparison baseline. The additional time after considering
synchronization should be an estimate of the overhead in
model inference. We tested different synchronization meth-
ods. The first is consecutive kernel launches in the naive
pytorch code. It also contains CPU overhead, so the value
is large. We used the CUDA graph to chain all kernels and
get a result of 1.72 ms, which is close to our experience. The
third approach is a “software barrier” approach that we will
explain below.
The traditional view of the CUDA programming model
says we cannot explicitly synchronize across all blocks, as
they may not live together at all. However, in practice if we
launch a number of blocks that equals the number of SMs,
we can make sure that all blocks run together and use global
memory to create a barrier. An example code (in Triton) is
as follows:
lock_goal += psize
tl.atomic_add(lock_ptr, 1)
while tl.atomic_or(lock_ptr, 0)\
< lock_goal:
pass
